title: Histone readers MLLT1 and MLLT3 concentrate AID to confer locus specificity.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed all 9 freely available Nature supplementary spreadsheets from static-content.springer.com (no login): SI Table 1 'AID targets' has 4 sheets with exact row counts I counted myself - CH12 mouse line 93 regions with translocation counts, 203 regions with mutation frequency, 198 non-redundant; mouse activated B cells 236 regions with an RPA-asymmetry odds ratio and 60 with translocation counts; human Ramos 57 regions with mutation rate; human SUDHL5 57 regions with mutation counts. All are AID-target (positive) regions only - no non-target regions anywhere. SI Table 5 is 105 per-sample amplicon mutation-frequency rows. Source-data sheets with many rows (MOESM6 sheet 2b, 11,272 rows; MOESM7 sheet 3a, 9,495 rows) are unlabelled sorted value vectors for violin plots with no gene or coordinate identifiers. In GEO I read the full series and one full sample record for GSE336466 (SuperSeries, 52 samples) = GSE336330 (ChIP-seq, 40 samples) + GSE336464 (TT-seq, 12 samples), and the file lists: processed data is bigWig coverage tracks only (8.5 GB + 1.8 GB tars; individual tracks 64-390 MB), no peak calls and no per-gene matrices. I confirmed the tracks are genuinely readable without download by issuing HTTP range requests on four of them: valid bigWig magic 0x888FFC26, version 4, mouse build with 66 contigs totalling 2,729,142,909 bases and human hg19 with 297 contigs totalling 3,234,834,689 bases, plus their real signal summaries (e.g. MLLT3 CH12 WT rep1 mean 3.925, max 612,200).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the biology (that MLLT1/MLLT3 loss abolishes AID activity, condensate formation, the AID-MLLT1 fusion rescue) comes from the abstract and the GEO series summaries only - the article itself is paywalled with no PubMed Central copy, so I could not read the methods, the data availability statement or the figure legends. I therefore could not check the supplementary row counts against any number stated in the paper's text.

a1_downloadable.note: Verified open: GEO GSE336466 tracks served over public FTP/HTTPS with working range requests, and all 9 Nature supplementary files fetched anonymously from static-content.springer.com. No login, no access application.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: For the only task this data supports - predict which genomic regions AID mutates - the supplementary tables list positives only: 203, 236, 57 and 57 AID-target regions, and zero non-target regions in any file. The negative class, and any label for the rest of the genome, would have to be built by importing mutation data from four other publications (Peycheva, Dai, Meng, Chiarle), matching coordinates across genome builds and cell types, and choosing a non-target set by hand.

a3_inputs_present.note: For the listed regions the inputs are literally columns (MLLT1_signal, MLLT3_signal). Genome-wide inputs exist only as 10.3 GB of bigWig coverage tracks that must be binned into per-region features first.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated inside each sheet (mutation frequency as a fraction, 'Mutation rate (x10-5)', raw mutation counts, translocation counts) and the ChIP signal normalisation is documented in GEO. But the four sheets use four different, non-comparable label units, so they cannot be pooled.

a5_enough_rows.note: Largest single comparable labelled block I counted is 203 CH12 regions with mutation frequency; the others are 236, 93, 60, 57 and 57 rows. The checklist needs ~1,500 labelled rows, or ~400 for classification - and classification is impossible anyway because every row is a positive.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 27 KB-595 KB spreadsheets; ~1.5-2 GB of bigWig tracks if you went genome-wide
a6_fits_laptop.note: Tables are trivial. I verified the tracks can be read by HTTP range request without downloading them whole, so even the genome-wide variant would stay well under 16 GB of memory.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Could not compare against the paper's text - it is paywalled with no PubMed Central copy. The supplementary tables are internally consistent and parsed cleanly, and GEO's sample counts (40 ChIP-seq + 12 TT-seq = 52) match the SuperSeries.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels are real measurements from other labs' sequencing (translocation capture and amplicon mutation sequencing in Peycheva, Dai, Meng, Chiarle), not model outputs. But the regions were pre-selected as AID targets by those same studies, so the row set is enriched by construction.

existing_models.name: Alvarez-Prado et al. 2018 (Journal of Experimental Medicine) predictor of AID off-target genes
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved - the journal page returned HTTP 403, so I have only the search summary: they sequenced >1,500 genomic regions in mouse germinal-centre B cells, found 275 AID-target genes, and trained a machine-learning model on molecular features, reporting high-density RNA polymerase II and Spt5 binding as the best predictors. No accuracy number verified.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not verified - I could not open the full text.

existing_models.name: DeepSHM, a convolutional network predicting somatic hypermutation from DNA sequence context (k-mers of 5-21 bases)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved beyond the bioRxiv abstract found in search, which reports improved accuracy over earlier mutability models and an extended DWRCT motif; no number verified.

backbone.name: None appropriate. A DNA language model such as Nucleotide Transformer or AlphaGenome could in principle embed the target regions, but with 203 labelled positive regions and no negatives there is nothing to fit a head on.
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would be enough for the data volume; the limit is sample size, not compute.
backbone.licence: GEO data is public domain; Nature supplementary files carry the article's copyright, and the article is paywalled.

integration.partner_dataset: The 2018 Journal of Experimental Medicine atlas of somatic hypermutation (>1,500 sequenced mouse regions, 275 AID targets, positives and negatives) would be the obvious partner, joined to this paper's MLLT1/MLLT3 occupancy tracks.
integration.join_key: Mouse genome coordinates (this paper is mm10; the 2018 atlas would likely need a coordinate liftover) and gene symbol.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does adding MLLT1 and MLLT3 occupancy to the chromatin features already known to mark AID targets improve prediction of which genes AID mutates - and if so, by how much?

controls.positive_control: The immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus must come out as the top-scoring region: in SI Table 1 Igha and Ighm carry the highest MLLT1 signal (617 for Ighm) and the most translocations (1,672 and 1,269).
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the mutation-frequency labels among the 203 CH12 regions and confirm any correlation collapses.
controls.external_validation: The human Ramos (57 regions) and SUDHL5 (57 regions) sheets are an independent species and cell type, so a mouse-trained relationship could be checked there - but both are far too small to be a test set.

honest_claim_h3: Among 203 genomic regions that other laboratories had already identified as AID targets, higher MLLT1 and MLLT3 occupancy is associated with higher mutation frequency - a statement about already-known targets only, which says nothing about the rest of the genome because no non-target region appears in any deposited file.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use chromatin-reader occupancy at a genomic region to predict how often the antibody-mutating enzyme AID mutates it.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example is a genomic region with the measured occupancy of two histone-reading proteins, MLLT1 and MLLT3, from the paper's chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing. I counted the usable examples: 203 regions in the mouse CH12 line, 236 in mouse activated B cells, 57 in human Ramos and 57 in human SUDHL5 - all of them known AID targets, with no non-target regions supplied.
plain_idea.predict: The mutation rate that AID causes at that region, measured by deep amplicon sequencing or by counting chromosome translocations, in each case by a different previously published study rather than by this paper.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Lymphoma biologists would like a way to flag which genes AID will damage, because AID off-target mutation drives B-cell lymphoma; a working predictor would tell them which loci to sequence. Even a failure would say whether these two proteins add anything beyond transcription-based predictors.

ml_idea: The project considered was: predict AID-induced mutation of a genomic region from MLLT1/MLLT3/RNA-polymerase-II/CDK9 occupancy, first as a regression over the paper's own target list and then genome-wide by binning the deposited coverage tracks. It dies on sample size and on the complete absence of negatives: the richest labelled table is 203 positive regions, so the only honest analysis is the scatter plot the authors already published. The genome-wide version would require importing labels from four other papers across two genome builds and inventing a negative set, which is exactly the label-construction failure the checklist warns about.

effort.compute_note: I actually did most of this: downloading and parsing all nine spreadsheets took minutes and under 1 GB of memory. The genome-wide variant would add roughly 1.5-2 GB of bigWig downloads and a few hours of binning, which I estimated rather than ran.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in SI Table 1 and look for a single non-target region. I did: 203 is the biggest block and there are zero negatives. That one count kills the project in ten minutes.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 and A2. The deposited data is 10.3 GB of chromatin coverage tracks plus supplementary tables that list only AID-target regions: the largest comparable labelled block is 203 rows, the other blocks are 236, 93, 60, 57 and 57 rows in four different non-comparable units across two species, and not one non-target region is provided anywhere, so the negative class and any genome-wide label would have to be constructed by importing mutation data from four other publications and matching coordinates across genome builds. The large source-data sheets that looked promising (11,272 and 9,495 rows) turned out to be unlabelled sorted value vectors for violin plots with no identifiers. This is a strong mechanistic cell-biology paper whose public data is designed to support figures, not models.
